wiki_topics.title: Agent benchmarks: fixed tasks that exercise real tool use
wiki_topics.summary:
Pin down a fixed set of tasks with known good outcomes and run agents against
them repeatedly. Unlike model benchmarks, agent benchmarks have to exercise
*tool use and multi-step trajectories* — booking, querying, fixing, coordinating
— so they double as integration tests for the whole agent, not just the model.

wiki_topics.title: Agent token costs are unpredictable and easily run away
wiki_topics.summary:
A chatbot turn costs a predictable number of tokens; an agent can loop, re-read
its whole context every step, spawn sub-agents, and call a model to grade its
own work — so the bill is a function of *behavior*, not request count, and a
single misbehaving run or a topology choice can multiply spend without anyone
noticing until the invoice arrives. Cost is the run-time obstacle that the
build-time decisions (memory, multi-agent, eval) silently determine.

wiki_topics.title: Measuring whether an agent actually worked is hard
wiki_topics.summary:
A chatbot is graded on its final answer; an agent has to be graded on what it
*did* — the multi-step trajectory of tool calls, retries, and decisions that
led there. Outputs are non-deterministic, "correct-looking" answers can come
from broken paths, and a benchmark the agent has effectively memorized tells
you nothing about a new environment. Knowing whether an agent works in
production is itself an unsolved engineering problem.

wiki_topics.title: Agents forget across steps and sessions
wiki_topics.summary:
An agent's working memory is its context window, which is finite and resets
between runs. On long-horizon tasks it forgets earlier steps, repeats work, and
loses the user's intent — so "agent memory" (what to persist, where, and how to
recall it) becomes a first-class architecture problem rather than a prompt tweak.

wiki_topics.title: Orchestration patterns: topologies, handoffs, and harnesses
wiki_topics.summary:
Orchestration is the control plane of a multi-agent system: how the work is
decomposed, which agent does what, how they hand off, and who — if anyone — is
in charge. The pattern you pick (central orchestrator vs. decentralized, a fixed
graph vs. one generated per task) sets the cost, latency, and reliability
ceiling of the whole system.

wiki_topics.title: Sandboxing, scoped credentials, and guardrails
wiki_topics.summary:
Assume the agent will be hijacked and limit the damage: run its code in a
sandbox, give it narrowly scoped and short-lived credentials, gate high-impact
actions behind approvals, and screen inputs/outputs with guardrails. None of
these stops injection on its own — together they shrink the blast radius of one
that gets through.

wiki_topics.title: Context compaction: summarize, compress, and curate the working set
wiki_topics.summary:
Keep memory *inside* the context window but small: summarize old turns,
compress history, and deliberately curate what stays in-context each step
("context engineering"). The agent forgets less because the working set is
chosen, not just truncated.

wiki_topics.title: Cost controls: budgets, metering, and per-task attribution
wiki_topics.summary:
Make agent spend observable and bounded: meter token usage per task, user, and
tool; attribute it to the unit of work (a request, a PR); set budgets and hard
caps so a runaway loop trips a limit instead of the invoice; and cut fixed
overhead with caching. These are the operational guardrails that sit *around* an
agent, complementing the architectural levers (compaction, topology, cheap
judges) that reduce the underlying token count.

wiki_topics.title: LLM-as-judge: model-graded evaluation of traces and outputs
wiki_topics.summary:
Use a model to grade a model: give an LLM the agent's output (or its full
trace), plus a rubric, and have it return a structured verdict. It scales the
judgment human raters can't keep up with — every production trace, every CI run —
and is the practical backbone of agent evaluation when answers are open-ended.

wiki_topics.title: Model Context Protocol: a standard interface for agent tools
wiki_topics.summary:
The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is a standard way to describe, discover, and
call tools so any MCP-speaking agent can use any MCP server. It collapses the
N×M problem of bespoke integrations into a common interface — the agent
equivalent of "speak HTTP" instead of writing a custom client per service.

wiki_topics.title: Agent behavior drifts as the model, SDK, and runtime churn under it
wiki_topics.summary:
An agent is built on a substrate you don't control and that moves faster than
your app: the underlying model gets upgraded or deprecated, the agent SDK and
orchestration framework ship multiple releases a week, and the serving runtime
changes its behavior under load. Every bump can silently change what the agent
does — or reintroduce a regression — between two deploys where *your* code never
changed. Drift is the run-time obstacle of maintenance: keeping a working agent
working as everything beneath it shifts.

wiki_topics.title: Coordinating multiple agents adds more failure than capability
wiki_topics.summary:
Splitting a job across several agents promises specialization and parallelism,
but every handoff is a lossy interface and each added agent multiplies the ways
the system can stall, loop, or disagree. Coordination overhead routinely eats
the gains — the hard part isn't building the agents, it's getting them to work
together without costing more than one good agent would.

wiki_topics.title: Untrusted input and tools can hijack an agent
wiki_topics.summary:
An agent treats whatever it reads — a web page, a tool result, a file, another
agent's message — as instructions it might follow. Prompt injection turns that
into an attack: hidden text redirects the agent to exfiltrate data, misuse its
tools, or escalate privileges. Because the agent has real credentials and can
act, a successful injection is not a bad answer — it's an unauthorized action.

wiki_topics.title: Agents reach the outside world through fragile, ad-hoc integrations
wiki_topics.summary:
An agent is only as useful as the tools it can call, but every integration has
historically been bespoke: hand-written wrappers around REST APIs, brittle
schemas the model misuses, and no shared way to discover or authorize tools.
Connecting an agent to real systems — infra, browsers, SaaS — is where a lot of
the engineering actually goes, and it breaks in production in ways the model
never sees.

wiki_topics.title: External knowledge base: vector and graph retrieval
wiki_topics.summary:
Push long-term memory *out* of the context window into an external store —
embeddings in a vector index, and/or a knowledge graph of entities and
relations — and retrieve only the relevant slice at each step. This is how an
agent "remembers" more than fits in a prompt.

wiki_topics.title: Version pinning, compatibility ranges, and staged upgrades
wiki_topics.summary:
Treat the model, agent SDK, framework, and serving runtime as version-controlled
dependencies, not a rolling stream: pin exact versions, declare the compatibility
range you actually support, heed deprecation warnings, and promote upgrades
through a staged, tested path instead of tracking latest. It doesn't stop the
substrate from changing — it stops the change from reaching production
unnoticed.

latest_playbook_cards.title: Pin governance constraints so compaction can't silently delete them
latest_playbook_cards.problem: Long-running agents summarize or evict context to stay under the token budget. When a policy or guardrail scrolls out of the live window, the agent stops obeying it — and there's no error, the rule just quietly vanishes from context.
latest_playbook_cards.apply: Treat governance constraints as non-evictable. Store hard rules (allowed tools, forbidden actions, approval gates) in a pinned region that your compaction/summarization step is forbidden to touch, and re-inject the verbatim constraint text into every post-compaction prompt rather than trusting the summary to carry it. Add a regression check that runs a prohibited action after a forced compaction and asserts the agent still refuses.

latest_playbook_cards.title: Don't force a JSON schema and tool-calling in the same decode pass
latest_playbook_cards.problem: Enabling structured-output (JSON Schema) constraints and tool calling together can make a model stop invoking tools entirely, even while it still produces schema-valid text. Grammar-based token masking from the schema makes the tool-invocation tokens unreachable during decoding, so the agent silently goes inert instead of acting.
latest_playbook_cards.apply: Split the work into two passes: let the model decide and emit tool calls in an unconstrained (or tool-grammar-only) decode, run the tools, then apply the JSON Schema constraint only to the final response-formatting pass. Never compile a response schema that masks the tokens your tool-call channel needs. If you're on a single-pass framework, verify on your own open-weight models that tools still fire with the schema attached before shipping.

latest_playbook_cards.title: Engineer recovery paths for flaky tools, not just happy-path calls
latest_playbook_cards.problem: Agents benchmarked on clean, trustworthy tools fall over when the real environment misbehaves — spec drift, malformed outputs, execution failures, stale data, or two sources that disagree. The failures trace to weak hazard diagnosis and ineffective recovery, not to running out of tool budget or thinking time.
latest_playbook_cards.apply: Stop assuming tools succeed. For each tool, define an explicit recovery policy: detect the hazard (timeout, schema mismatch, empty/contradictory result), then retry, fall back to an alternate tool/source, verify the output, or cross-check two sources before trusting it. Inject these recovery hints into the system prompt and test them by deliberately corrupting tool responses in a staging harness — measure task completion under faults, not just function-call accuracy.

latest_playbook_cards.title: Audit your LLM judge for position and language bias before trusting its scores
latest_playbook_cards.problem: If you grade agent runs with an LLM-as-a-judge, the judge carries systematic biases that raw accuracy hides: it favors whichever answer sits in slot A, prefers longer responses, flips its verdict when you swap the order, and degrades sharply on lower-resource languages. A judge that looks accurate in aggregate can be near-random where it matters.
latest_playbook_cards.apply: Stop reporting judge accuracy alone. For every pairwise comparison, run it twice with the candidate order swapped and only count verdicts that are order-consistent; control for response length so verbosity doesn't leak in as quality; and run a per-language reliability check before you trust scores on non-English trajectories. Use a degradation-based gold set (perturb a known-good answer to build ground-truth pairs) so you can measure these biases without human annotation.

latest_playbook_cards.title: Measure reasoning-token usage, not just latency, before shipping a quantized reasoner
latest_playbook_cards.problem: Low-bit (INT4/INT3) quantization is sold as cheaper inference, but for reasoning models the savings can evaporate: the quantized model often produces a longer chain of thought to reach the same answer, so the per-token speedup is offset by generating more tokens. Accuracy charts and per-token latency both miss this hidden test-time compute cost.
latest_playbook_cards.apply: When you evaluate a quantized reasoning model for an agent step, report total reasoning-token usage alongside accuracy and end-to-end latency on your own workload — not just per-token throughput. Compare full-precision vs quantized on tokens-to-answer for representative tasks before assuming the smaller model is cheaper, and prefer quantization-aware training over naive post-training quantization where you control the model.

latest_playbook_cards.title: Stop re-encoding the same frames: reuse multimodal KV cache across look-backs
latest_playbook_cards.problem: Multimodal agents re-examine the same video frames, UI screenshots, and rendered artifacts every time the context window slides or reasoning iterates — and standard prefix caches only reuse content at a fixed leading position, so each look-back re-encodes from scratch. Naively reusing the cache instead drops cross-chunk conditioning and halves multi-hop reasoning accuracy.
latest_playbook_cards.apply: For agents that repeatedly revisit the same visual artifacts, adopt position-invariant KV reuse: cache each image/frame chunk position-free, then on reuse re-rotate it (RoPE) to the target position and apply a small low-rank conditioning patch that restores cross-chunk binding. That lets you reorder cached chunks, relocate survivors of a sliding window by rotation only, and rehydrate evicted chunks from their patch — all without re-encoding — instead of paying full re-prefill on every look-back.

latest_playbook_cards.title: Turn agent traces into durable memory with a capture → analyze → update loop
latest_playbook_cards.problem: Agents that start every run from a blank slate keep repeating the same mistakes and need the same corrections, because nothing learned in one trajectory persists into the next. Dumping whole conversation histories into a memory store instead bloats context and buries the few durable lessons under noise.
latest_playbook_cards.apply: Build an explicit three-step loop. Capture full traces (decisions, tool calls, outcomes). Analyze them to surface recurring failures and reusable patterns. Then selectively extract only durable context — semantic facts/preferences, episodic examples, and procedural rules/workflows — into long-term memory, leaving raw history behind. Critically, make agents actually reload updated memory at runtime (cached prompts and tool definitions need an explicit refresh), and gate memory writes behind an eval so a bad update can't silently regress behavior.
